paras: The whipping of Jim Pruitt was an attack by a band of white men, called "white cappers" in the press, on a Black man in the Cross Anchor section of Spartanburg County, South Carolina, on a Tuesday night in late May 1903. The men took Pruitt from his house, whipped him severely and threatened him and his wife with death if they spoke of it. The case became known when the couple complained to a magistrate in Spartanburg, and a dispatch about it ran in several South Carolina weeklies.

According to a Spartanburg dispatch to The State, "some white men" came to Pruitt's house on a Tuesday night, took him out and whipped him on his bare limbs, leaving him so lacerated and bruised that he was "scarcely able to walk." The attackers threatened Pruitt and his wife, Alma Pruitt, with death "if they made any mention of the lawless occurrence." Neither of them knew why he had been whipped, and no accusation against him appears in the coverage.

Despite the threat, the Pruitts travelled to Spartanburg on a Thursday afternoon and told their story at the office of Magistrate Kirby. Kirby referred them by letter to Magistrate Mike Patton at Cross Anchor, who, the dispatch said, would "doubtless investigate the case and put an end to such proceedings." No report of an investigation, arrest or prosecution was found.

The Newberry Herald and News printed the earliest notice found, on 2 June, a brief paraphrase that called Pruitt's account "a pitiful tale" and noted that "the negro could assign no cause for such punishment." The fuller State dispatch, headed "Whipped by White Caps," appeared word for word in The Batesburg Advocate and The Manning Times on 3 June and in The Marlboro Democrat on 5 June. Its tone was mixed: it described a "pitiful tale of misery" and a "lawless occurrence" while remarking that Pruitt "was certainly well flogged." No coverage in the Black press was found.

The date is uncertain: the dispatch places the whipping on "last Tuesday night" but also says Pruitt reached Spartanburg "one week later," while the Newberry paper says the beating happened "several days before" his visit. If the Thursday visit was 28 May, the whipping took place on 19 or 26 May.

framing.detail: The State dispatch, headed 'Whipped by White Caps', called the whipping a 'lawless occurrence' and hoped the magistrate would 'put an end to such proceedings', while remarking that Pruitt 'was certainly well flogged'.
The Newberry Herald and News gave a brief note calling it 'a pitiful tale' and referring to Pruitt as 'the negro'.

conflicts.note: The dispatch is internally inconsistent: 'last Tuesday night' suggests two days before the Thursday visit, 'one week later' suggests nine. If the visit was Thursday 28 May (A1, dated 2 June, says 'last week'), the whipping was 26 or 19 May.
